Baby & Child

Congenital hand differences in babies and children

Updated: November 14, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When a newborn has joined fingers, an extra thumb or a hand that looks different from the other one, families often want to know what that child will be able to do. A useful first step is to ask the newborn team to examine both hands and arms and arrange a pediatric hand appointment. Feeling, movement, grip and the way the two hands work together tell a family more about future activities than the number or shape of the fingers alone.

What the first examination can tell you

A clinician checks where the difference starts, which joints move, how the baby moves the arm spontaneously and whether blood is reaching the fingers. A small hand may have a strong, mobile thumb. An extra thumb may look well formed on the surface while sharing a joint with its neighbor. The team may use an X-ray to see the bones and how they connect. A difference first seen on a pregnancy scan is assessed again after birth.

Some differences occur on their own and some run in families. A pattern involving both arms, several stiff joints or other parts of the body may prompt further examination or a genetics referral. For example, joined fingers can occur in Apert syndrome alongside characteristic skull changes. BeMama covers that diagnosis at https://bemamas.com/newborn/apert-syndrome/ Isolated webbing has other explanations. If the family has questions about another pregnancy, a precise diagnosis is a better starting point than a photograph of another child.

How clinicians describe a hand difference

The descriptions a family hears may refer to how a hand formed, which structures are present, or how they move. Fingers may be joined, duplicated, underdeveloped or enlarged. A constriction ring has a different origin from a finger that grew short. A child may also have a broader bone or joint condition, such as arthrogryposis, in which several joints can be stiff from birth. Different classification systems serve different purposes.

Ask the clinician to point out the relevant structures on your child's hand or X-ray. Learn which part can bend actively and which can move with gentle assistance during the examination. These observations can help explain why two hands that look alike may need different care. Many families never receive a single explanation for why a hand developed as it did. An unexpected finding at birth is no reason to blame a parent's ordinary activities during pregnancy.

A short forearm or a small or missing thumb

The radius is the forearm bone on the thumb side. If this side developed incompletely, the forearm may be short, the wrist may lean toward the thumb side, and the thumb can be small or absent. Ulnar longitudinal deficiency affects the little-finger side of the forearm, where the ulna may be short or absent. The elbow, wrist and fingers can contribute differently to what the child can reach or hold. Other children are born with a limb that ends before the wrist or fingers.

A baby who uses the little-finger side to grasp may already have a useful strategy. The team can watch how the baby brings an object toward the mouth before suggesting a change in wrist position. A hand therapist may demonstrate gentle exercises or fit a splint. Some children benefit from a procedure to improve wrist position or thumb function. Follow-up depends on joint mobility, the rest of the arm, growth and the child's health. A change in wrist shape on its own does not set a surgical deadline.

Joined fingers and extra fingers

Joined fingers are called syndactyly. In simple syndactyly, skin and other soft tissue link the fingers. In complex syndactyly, the bones are connected too. Complete webbing extends to the fingertips. Incomplete webbing stops partway along the fingers. These terms answer separate questions, so complete webbing can still be simple. The surgeon looks at which fingers share tissue, how their lengths differ and whether continued growth might pull one out of alignment.

Polydactyly means an additional digit or part of one. It can occur next to the thumb or little finger, or between other fingers. An extra digit can range from a small skin attachment to a finger with bones and working joints. A duplicated thumb may need reconstruction to give the child one stable thumb that moves well. Ask how tendons and joints are shared. Have even a small extra digit assessed and leave it intact for that visit. Cutting or tying it off at home can injure the baby.

A finger that stays bent

A contracture means a joint has limited movement and cannot fully reach a position, such as straightening all the way. The skin, joints or tissues responsible for movement may be involved. A thumb that clicks or locks can have another explanation. In pediatric trigger thumb, the tendon that bends the thumb catches as it passes through a narrow pulley near the thumb's base. A caregiver may first notice the tip stays bent when the toddler opens the hand.

The clinician asks when the catching began, whether it hurts and which activities have changed. A child with a painless trigger thumb that works well may be observed because it can improve with time. Persistent locking, pain or trouble using the hand can lead to a discussion of surgical release. Keep a note of when it happens and let the clinician examine it. Repeatedly forcing the thumb straight is uncomfortable and does not establish the diagnosis.

Short or missing fingers and everyday grasp

A small thumb may have a narrow web space, weak muscles, an unstable joint or missing bones. A child with symbrachydactyly may have short fingers, webbing or small soft-tissue nubs where fingers usually develop. Some children have good control of a short hand and need little help. Watch what happens when the child tries to steady a cup or hold a toy in one hand while adjusting it with the other.

Occupational therapy can build on the child's own grip. An adapted handle may make one activity easier, while changing the position of the object works for another. If an unstable thumb makes it hard to pinch, reconstruction may improve stability or movement. For a missing or very underdeveloped thumb, one option is repositioning the index finger to serve as a thumb. A family considering this operation can ask to see how the proposed pinch would differ from the child's current one.

When one or more fingers are much larger

Macrodactyly is overgrowth involving several tissues within a digit, including bone and soft tissue. More than one finger can be affected. In a static pattern, the larger digit grows roughly in step with the other fingers. In a progressive pattern, the size difference increases. A baby may be comfortable with a wider finger and later find that it crowds the neighboring fingers or catches on clothing. A sudden increase in swelling calls for assessment and should not be assumed to be ordinary growth.

Following growth and movement over time helps the family and team weigh the benefits of treatment. Options for selected children include reducing bulky tissue or limiting future bone length. A procedure aimed at length does not also control width. In severe progressive cases where one digit interferes with the use of the rest of the hand, removing that digit may be discussed alongside its alternatives. Ask about likely changes in grip, the possibility of repeated procedures and how much motion can realistically be preserved.

A constriction ring needs a circulation check

An amniotic band can leave a groove around a finger, hand or limb as it develops before birth. A shallow groove may have little effect. A deeper band can compress nerves or interfere with blood flow and fluid drainage, leaving swelling beyond the groove. A part of a finger can be missing, or injured fingertips can join as they heal before birth. Bands sometimes affect other limbs or, rarely, the face or body. A foot or facial difference needs its own assessment.

If a newborn's finger beyond a tight ring is becoming very swollen, pale, blue or cold, tell the birth team immediately or seek emergency care. Do not wait for a routine hand appointment or try to cut into the groove. A band threatening circulation can require urgent surgical release. A stable shallow ring with healthy tissues beyond it may instead be monitored. The urgent question is whether the tissues are receiving blood now.

Choosing therapy, a device or surgery

Ask the team to name one activity a proposed treatment should make easier. Occupational therapy may help with dressing, feeding and using both hands together. Physical therapy may address arm movement where that affects reach. Splints should be fitted for the child, with directions on wear and skin checks. A prosthesis replaces a missing part and may help with a specific activity. Families can ask to try an adaptive tool or watch the child attempt the same task without a device.

Surgery has different purposes. Separating a web may give fingers room to grow and move independently. A skin graft can cover an area left exposed after separation. A tendon transfer can give a weak thumb a new direction of pull. An external frame is an option in selected cases to gradually change bone length or alignment. Ask what recovery would require, whether another procedure might be needed with growth and what could happen if the family chooses observation. Include the child's preferences as they become able to express them.

What to bring to follow-up

Think of a task that matters to the child today. A toddler might want to feed themself with a spoon, while an older child might be working on fastening a jacket or holding a bicycle handlebar. Tell the therapist which part of the task is difficult and what the child already does successfully. It is also worth mentioning discomfort, difficulty fitting a splint and any change in movement.

Before leaving, ask when the next review is due and which changes warrant an earlier call. After any procedure, use the team's own cast, dressing and activity instructions. A new loss of finger color or warmth, marked swelling, or increasing pain under a cast or dressing warrants urgent medical attention. An agreed contact route lets the family act promptly if the hand changes between visits.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the pediatric hand team which structures the difference affects and whether any other examinations are needed.

Choose a treatment goal the child can use in daily life and revisit it as their skills and priorities change.

Ask for individual instructions on splints, exercises, recovery and signs that circulation needs immediate attention.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help families prepare questions and keep track of activities their child finds difficult. The hand team can examine movement, identify the tissues involved and advise on treatment.

When to seek help

Get emergency care for a cold, pale, blue or markedly swollen finger beyond a tight constriction ring. Have an extra finger or persistently bent joint assessed before attempting any treatment. Follow the treating team’s instructions for casts and splints.

Evidence notes updated: November 14, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Arrange a pediatric hand assessment to understand the bones, joints, movement and circulation behind a visible difference.
  • Joined fingers, extra digits, undergrowth, overgrowth and constriction rings have different effects on grip and growth.
  • The way a child uses both hands during an everyday task helps guide therapy, equipment and surgical choices.
  • Ask what an operation is expected to change, how recovery works and what following the hand without surgery would involve.
  • A pale, blue, cold or markedly swollen finger beyond a tight ring needs immediate assessment.

Frequently asked questions

What should we do after our baby is born with a hand difference?

Ask the newborn clinician to examine the hand and arrange follow-up with a pediatric hand team. Ask whether the baby needs a circulation assessment immediately and what can wait for the specialist visit. A clear description and a follow-up date can help even when the final diagnosis takes time.

What types of differences can be present at birth?

Some fingers are joined, extra, smaller, absent or larger than expected. A forearm bone can also be affected, or a constriction ring may encircle part of the limb. Sometimes the hand is part of a broader skeletal or joint condition. The specialist can explain which description best fits the child.

What is overgrowth of a baby's finger?

Macrodactyly means that tissues within one or more digits grow larger than expected. The team follows whether the size difference stays proportional or increases as the child grows and checks movement and comfort. Decisions about treatment depend on how the enlarged digit affects the entire hand.

How are congenital hand differences treated?

Some children need observation only. Others benefit from therapy, an individually fitted splint, an adapted tool, a prosthesis or surgery. Ask what specific improvement each option offers for your child's current or developing skills. Several treatments may be used at different stages.

Can an extra thumb simply be removed?

An extra thumb can share bones, joints, ligaments or tendons with its neighbor. The surgeon examines how both parts move and may use an X-ray to plan reconstruction. The aim is a stable thumb the child can use to grasp and pinch. Leave any extra digit for the clinical team to assess.

Does webbing mean our child has a syndrome?

Many children have joined fingers as their only finding. The examination and family history help determine whether a wider assessment is useful. Finger webbing alone cannot tell a family whether a particular genetic condition is present or what the chance of recurrence might be.

Should we stretch a bent finger ourselves?

Ask for an examination before starting exercises. A hand therapist can show the direction, pressure and frequency of any movement appropriate to the child's condition. Avoid forcing a stiff or catching joint and ask for review if it becomes painful or the child uses it less.

When does a ring around a finger need emergency care?

A cold, pale or blue digit or pronounced swelling beyond a tight ring can indicate impaired circulation. Alert the newborn team immediately or seek emergency care. A stable groove with normal circulation can be assessed on a different timetable chosen by the treating team.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
